title: Episode 324: George I: The German Elector, the South Sea Bubble, and Sir Robert Walpole
description:
The consequential, misunderstood reign of King George I, the first British monarch of the House of Hanover. Bypassing over fifty Catholic claimants under the Act of Settlement, fifty-four-year-old Elector Georg Ludwig of Hanover arrived in London in 1714 speaking fluent French and German but little English. Crushing the Jacobite Rising of 1715, George navigated the catastrophic financial collapse of the South Sea Bubble in 1720, turning to Sir Robert Walpole to restore national credit. With George preferring Hanover and conducting council meetings in French or Latin, executive power shifted permanently to the Cabinet, establishing Walpole as Britain's first Prime Minister. Discover the founder of the Hanoverian dynasty.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the foreign prince who transformed the constitutional architecture of Great Britain: a sovereign who spoke little English, yet under whose reign the modern office of Prime Minister was born: King George I. Here is George with the story of the first Hanoverian.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ELECTOR OF HANOVER: HERRENHAUSEN TO GREENWICH: 1660 TO 1714
Born in May 1660 at Osnabrück in northern Germany, Georg Ludwig was the eldest son of Ernst August, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and Sophia of the Palatinate, granddaughter of King James I. Reared in the militarized German princely states during the height of the Ottoman and French wars, George was a seasoned, courageous soldier who fought alongside the Holy Roman Emperor at the Siege of Vienna in 1683. In 1682, George married his cousin, Sophia Dorothea of Celle, for territorial consolidation. The marriage was an unmitigated personal disaster: when Sophia Dorothea engaged in a scandalous affair with the dashing Swedish Count Philip Christoph von Königsmarck, Königsmarck was mysteriously assassinated in the palace at Hanover, and George divorced Sophia Dorothea, imprisoning her in the fortress of Ahlden Castle for thirty-two years until her death. In 1698, George became Elector of Hanover, governing his German principality with exemplary fiscal prudence from his Baroque palace of Herrenhausen, taking immense pride in its grand fountains and hedge mazes. The tragic fate of Sophia Dorothea of Celle remained the darkest scandal of George's private life. Königsmarck, a handsome Swedish nobleman, had wooed the lonely, neglected electress, plotting to help her escape from Hanover. On the night of July 1, 1694, Königsmarck was intercepted leaving the Leineschloss palace by four of the Elector's guards, run through with swords, and his body dumped into the river or buried beneath palace floorboards. For thirty-two years, Sophia Dorothea was locked in the moated castle of Ahlden, forbidden from seeing her children or remarrying, allowed to ride her carriage only within a two-mile perimeter under armed guard. This cold, unforgiving severity earned George the enduring hatred of his son George Augustus and the horror of British society.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE ACT OF SETTLEMENT AND THE VOYAGE TO BRITAIN: SEPTEMBER 1714
When Queen Anne died in August 1714, the British Parliament enacted the most radical dynastic engineering in world history. Under the 1701 Act of Settlement, over fifty closer Catholic relatives—including James II's exiled son, the Old Pretender—were disqualified on religious grounds, leaving fifty-four-year-old George as the closest Protestant heir. On September 18, 1714, George landed at Greenwich through thick autumn fog aboard the royal yacht Peregrine, accompanied by his son George Augustus and a retinue of German courtiers and Turkish valets, Mahomet and Mustapha. Crowned at Westminster Abbey in October in a ceremony conducted largely in Latin because the King spoke minimal English and his Whig ministers spoke no German, George was greeted with skepticism by Londoners. Satirists mocked his two German mistresses, the tall, gaunt Melusine von der Schulenburg, whom Londoners nicknamed 'the Maypole', and the corpulent Sophia von Kielmansegg, nicknamed 'the Elephant'. Yet George was an experienced, pragmatic European ruler who understood his limited constitutional role. George I's coronation at Westminster Abbey was a linguistic comedy of errors: because the German king knew very little English and the Whig ministers knew no German, proceedings were conducted in broken, kitchen Latin, with both sides frequently misunderstanding ceremonial instructions. Outside the abbey, Jacobite riots erupted in London, Bristol, and Norwich, with crowds shouting 'No Hanover! High Church and Ormond!' Yet George was far from a dullard: he was an accomplished mathematician, a patron of George Frideric Handel—who composed the magnificent Water Music for the King's royal barge progress on the Thames in 1717—and a monarch of calm, unflappable dignity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE 'FIFTEEN': THE JACOBITE RISING OF 1715
The Hanoverian succession was immediately challenged in September 1715 by the Jacobite Rising, known as 'The Fifteen'. John Erskine, Earl of Mar, raised the Stuart standard in the Scottish Highlands, rallying ten thousand Highland clansmen to restore James Francis Edward Stuart, the 'Old Pretender'. Concurrently, northern English Catholic gentry rose in Northumberland. But the rebellion was fatally mismanaged: the English Jacobites were surrounded and surrendered at the Battle of Preston in Lancashire, while Mar's Highland army fought a bloody, indecisive stalemate against the Duke of Argyll's Hanoverian forces at Sheriffmuir in November. When the Old Pretender finally landed at Peterhead in December, he was melancholic, uninspiring, and lacked money and arms. By February 1716, as Hanoverian reinforcements advanced through the winter snows, James fled back to France aboard a small ship from Montrose. George I acted with calculated firmness: while key Jacobite lords like the Earl of Derwentwater were beheaded on Tower Hill, the King pardoned hundreds of common prisoners, securing his throne against domestic rebellion. The Jacobite Rising of 1715 was doomed by the military incompetence of the Earl of Mar, affectionately satirized as 'Bobbing John' for his shifting loyalties. Despite having an army that vastly outnumbered government forces in Scotland, Mar hesitated at Sheriffmuir, allowing the Duke of Argyll to hold the field. When James Francis Edward Stuart arrived, he suffered from severe depression and toothache, failing to inspire his Highland followers, remarking mournfully that he had come to share their funeral rather than celebrate a triumph. George I's firm suppression of the rebellion, followed by the Disarming Act and the construction of military roads across the Highlands by General George Wade, firmly consolidated the Hanoverian dynasty upon the British throne.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SOUTH SEA BUBBLE: FINANCIAL CATACLYSM: 1720
In 1720, Great Britain was rocked by the first colossal stock market crash in financial history: the South Sea Bubble. The South Sea Company, founded to trade slaves and goods with Spanish America, proposed an audacious scheme to assume thirty-one million pounds of Britain's national debt in exchange for exclusive trading monopolies and stock conversions. Speculative hysteria gripped London: aristocrats, politicians, clergymen, and ordinary citizens crowded into Exchange Alley to buy shares, which skyrocketed from one hundred and twenty-eight pounds in January to over one thousand pounds in August. The royal court was deeply implicated: George I's German mistresses and ministers accepted corrupt bribes of unissued stock. When the unsustainable speculative bubble burst in September 1720, share prices collapsed to one hundred and thirty-five pounds in weeks. Thousands of families were ruined, suicides swept London, and public fury threatened to overthrow both the government and the Hanoverian monarchy. The South Sea Bubble exposed the raw venality and speculative mania of early Georgian capitalism. Promoters launched absurd joint-stock companies in Exchange Alley, including schemes to extract silver from lead, build floating mansions, and most famously, 'a company for carrying on an undertaking of great advantage, but nobody to know what it is', which collected thousands of pounds in deposits before the promoter vanished overnight. When the bubble burst, Sir Isaac Newton, who lost twenty thousand pounds in South Sea stock, famously remarked: 'I can calculate the motions of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.' George I himself had made profits on early share sales, narrowly avoiding public disgrace.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: SIR ROBERT WALPOLE AND THE BIRTH OF THE PRIME MINISTER
In the midst of the financial catastrophe, King George turned to Sir Robert Walpole, a genial, shrewd Norfolk squire and financial genius. Appointed First Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer in April 1721, Walpole implemented the 'Screening' operation: he restructured the ruined company's debts, dividing the loss between the Bank of England and the East India Company, while shielding the Royal Family and ministers from public prosecution. Walpole restored national credit and stabilized the British economy. Because George I preferred residing in Hanover—spending nearly a fifth of his reign abroad—and found British parliamentary debates tedious, the King stopped attending regular Cabinet meetings. In the King's absence, Walpole chaired the meetings, coordinated government policy, and commanded majorities in the House of Commons through patronage and political management. Walpole thus became Britain's first 'Prime Minister', permanently shifting executive governing power from the royal bedchamber to Downing Street. Sir Robert Walpole's political genius lay in his earthy, cynical understanding of human nature: he famously observed of parliamentarians, 'All those men have their price.' Operating from 10 Downing Street—which George I gifted to Walpole in 1735 as an official residence for the First Lord of the Treasury—Walpole established cabinet solidarity, insisting that all ministers publicly support government policy or resign. Walpole avoided costly foreign wars, kept land taxes low for country squires, and coined the famous maxim of British political stability: 'Quieta non movere'—'Let sleeping dogs lie.' Through his twenty-one years as Britain's first Prime Minister, Walpole forged the constitutional machinery of modern British parliamentary democracy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE FAMILY FEUD: FATHER AND SON AT LEICESTER HOUSE
A persistent curse of the Hanoverian dynasty was the toxic, venomous hatred between fathers and their sons. George I despised his eldest son, George Augustus, Prince of Wales, who was popular, fluent in English, and fiercely protective of his imprisoned mother Sophia Dorothea. The feud exploded into public scandal in November 1717 at the christening of the Prince's newborn son: when the Prince quarreled violently with the Duke of Newcastle, whom the King had appointed godfather, King George placed his son under house arrest and banished him from St. James's Palace. The Prince of Wales established a rival court at Leicester House, which became the headquarters for opposition Whig and Tory politicians plotting against the King's government. This established the enduring Hanoverian political pattern: the heir to the throne always sided with the parliamentary opposition against his father, dividing the political establishment. The feud between George I and the Prince of Wales at Leicester House was an embarrassing public spectacle that paralyzed London society. The King issued a royal decree forbidding anyone who attended the Prince's court from being received at St. James's Palace, forcing aristocrats to choose between father and son. The Princess of Wales, Caroline of Ansbach, used her dazzling salon at Leicester House to patronize poets like Alexander Pope and John Gay, transforming the opposition court into the cultural center of London, ridiculing the King's stiff German mistresses and parsimonious court habits, deepening the family rift until Walpole brokered an uneasy public reconciliation in 1720.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE FINAL JOURNEY: OSNABRÜCK AND THE HANOVERIAN FOUNDATION: 1727
In June 1727, sixty-seven-year-old King George I set out from London on his sixth journey home to his beloved electorate of Hanover. Travelling across the Dutch countryside, the King was in high spirits, but on the road between Delden and Nordhorn on June 9, he suffered a severe stroke in his carriage, his face becoming paralyzed. When his courtiers urged stopping at the nearest town for medical treatment, the King stubbornly muttered in German: 'Osnabrück! Osnabrück!'—desperate to reach his birthplace. Arriving at the Prince-Bishop's Palace in Osnabrück, George I was carried into his bedchamber, where he died on June 11, 1727. He was buried in the chapel of Leine Castle in Hanover, the only British monarch since 1066 to be buried outside the British Isles. George I was never deeply loved by his British subjects, yet his pragmatism, emotional detachment, and constitutional restraint had allowed parliamentary cabinet government to take root, securing the Protestant succession. When George I suffered his fatal stroke in his carriage near Osnabrück, his passing marked the quiet completion of Britain's constitutional revolution. By leaving the day-to-day administration of the realm to his Cabinet and Parliament, George I had unwittingly facilitated the transition from royal personal rule to modern constitutional monarchy. The British Crown had become an institution that reigned rather than ruled, preserving national stability while allowing the dynamic commercial, maritime, and intellectual energies of the British people to build the richest empire on earth.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories.
